flashcards.q: Describe the cellular mechanism of auxin-induced stem elongation during phototropism.
flashcards.a: Unidirectional light causes auxin to migrate to the shaded side of the stem. Auxin binds to membrane receptors, activating proton pumps that pump H+ out of the cell into the cell wall. The acidic environment loosens the cell wall fibers, water enters by osmosis, increasing turgor pressure, and the cells elongate, causing the stem to bend toward the light.

flashcards.q: Identify the gaseous plant hormone and outline its major physiological roles.
flashcards.a: Ethylene is the gaseous plant hormone. It stimulates cellulase to promote abscission (leaf, fruit, or flower drop), accelerates fruit ripening (softening and flavor/odor production), inhibits axillary buds, and suppresses stem/root elongation.

flashcards.q: Contrast the roles of gibberellins and abscisic acid (ABA) in seed dormancy.
flashcards.a: Abscisic acid (ABA) acts as a stress hormone that initiates and maintains seed and bud dormancy to prevent germination in unfavorable conditions. In contrast, gibberellins break dormancy, promoting germination and stem elongation.

7.outline_blanks: Plants coordinate growth using chemical signals. Stems bend toward light because [[auxin]] accumulates on the shady side, activating [[proton pumps]] to loosen cell walls. During water stress, [[abscisic acid]] triggers stomatal closure, while the gaseous hormone [[ethylene]] stimulates cellulase to promote fruit ripening and leaf abscission.

7.title: Plant Tropisms
cheat_card: Phototropism: Growth toward unidirectional light. Cells on the shady side elongate due to auxin. Sensed by membrane pigment phototropin absorbing blue light.

Gravitropism: Growth in response to gravity. Sensed by statoliths (starch grains in amyloplasts) settling to the gravity-facing side of cells. Stems show negative gravitropism (grow up); roots show positive (grow down).
Thigmotropism: Growth in response to touch (e.g., coiling of tendrils). Thigmomorphogenesis is the entire plant's response to environmental stimuli like wind/rain.
Nastic movements: Reversible, growth-independent movements driven by turgor pressure (e.g., Venus flytrap closing or Mimosa folding) in response to non-directional stimuli.
Photoperiodism: Seasonal physiological responses regulated by day/night length changes using the photoreceptor phytochrome, which exists in inactive Pr (red) and active Pfr (far-red) forms.
7.memory_anchor:
Phytochrome Photoreceptor Interconversion

  • Pr (Inactive Red-Absorbing Form) → [Absorbs Red Light (660nm) during day] → Pfr (Active Far-Red-Absorbing Form)
  • Pfr (Active Far-Red-Absorbing Form) → [Absorbs Far-Red Light (730nm) or reverts in darkness] → Pr (Inactive)
  • Role: Triggers physiological responses such as seed germination and flowering relative to night length.

flashcards.q: Explain the mechanism and sensory structures responsible for plant gravitropism.
flashcards.a: Gravitropism depends on statoliths, which are dense starch grains located in amyloplasts. Under gravity, statoliths settle to the lower side of the cell. This physical settling tells the cell which way is down, redistributing auxin to regulate differential growth (downward in roots, upward in shoots).

flashcards.q: What are nastic movements and how do they differ from tropisms?
flashcards.a: Nastic movements are rapid, reversible movements driven by turgor pressure changes (water entering/leaving cells) in response to non-directional stimuli (like touch or temperature, e.g., Mimosa folding). Unlike tropisms, they do not involve growth and are independent of the direction of the stimulus.

flashcards.q: Explain how the active and inactive forms of phytochrome regulate photoperiodism.
flashcards.a: Phytochrome is a photoreceptor that exists in two interconvertible forms: inactive red (Pr) and active far-red (Pfr). Pr absorbs red light during the day and is converted to Pfr, which triggers physiological responses like germination and flowering. In darkness, Pfr slowly reverts back to Pr, allowing the plant to measure the length of the night.

7.outline_blanks: Plants respond to gravity using gravity-sensing starch grains called [[statoliths]]. Light responses are mediated by [[phototropin]] absorbing blue light, while seasonal responses like flowering are regulated by [[phytochrome]], which alternates between the inactive [[Pr]] and active [[Pfr]] forms.

7.title: Animal Tissues
cheat_card: Epithelial Tissue: Forms continuous sheets lining body cavities, anchored to a basement membrane. Classifed as simple (one layer: squamous, cuboidal, columnar) or stratified, joined by tight, adhesion, or gap junctions.

Connective Tissue: Consists of specialized cells in a noncellular ground substance with protein fibers (collagen, reticular, elastic). Categories: fibrous (loose, adipose, dense in tendons/ligaments), supportive (cartilage in lacunae; bone in lacunae within concentric circles of osteons around central canals), and fluid (blood, lymph).

Muscular Tissue: Contractile fibers containing actin and myosin. Skeletal is voluntary and striated; smooth is involuntary and non-striated; cardiac is striated, involuntary, and joined by intercalated disks.
Nervous Tissue: Conducts electrical impulses. Contains neurons (cell body, dendrites, axon) and supporting neuroglia (microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes).
7.memory_anchor:
Four Animal Tissue Types Overview

  • Epithelial: Protection & Lining (Connected to basement membrane; simple/stratified squamous, cuboidal, columnar).
  • Connective: Support & Transport (Cells in ground matrix; fibrous, supportive [cartilage/bone], fluid [blood/lymph]).
  • Muscular: Movement (Contractile actin/myosin; skeletal [striated, voluntary], smooth [non-striated, involuntary], cardiac [striated, intercalated disks]).
  • Nervous: Communication (Impulse conduction; neurons and supporting glial cells [neuroglia]).

flashcards.q: Contrast simple squamous, simple cuboidal, and simple columnar epithelial tissues.
flashcards.a: All three are single layers of cells touching the basement membrane. Simple squamous epithelia consist of flattened cells optimized for diffusion; simple cuboidal epithelia have cube-shaped cells optimized for secretion/absorption; simple columnar epithelia have tall, column-shaped cells optimized for absorption and lining the digestive tract.

flashcards.q: Describe the microanatomy of compact bone tissue.
flashcards.a: Compact bone contains structural units called osteons. Within each osteon, inorganic calcium salts and protein fibers are deposited in concentric circles around a central canal (which contains blood vessels). Mature bone cells (osteocytes) reside within small chambers called lacunae.

flashcards.q: Compare skeletal, smooth, and cardiac muscular tissues structurally and functionally.
flashcards.a: Skeletal muscle is voluntary, striated, and composed of long, multinucleated fibers. Smooth muscle is involuntary, spindle-shaped, and lacks striations. Cardiac muscle is striated but involuntary, consists of branching cells bound by intercalated disks, and contracts rhythmically via pacemaker cells.

7.outline_blanks: Animal organs are composed of four tissue types. Epithelial tissue is anchored to a [[basement membrane]], supportive connective tissue includes bone organized into [[osteons]], and muscular tissue contains contractile [[actin and myosin]] filaments. Nervous tissue consists of conducting cells called [[neurons]] and supporting cells called [[neuroglia]].

7.title: Circulatory System
cheat_card: Circulatory systems move fluid through the body, either open (hemolymph in hemocoel cavity) or closed (blood in vessels). Arteries carry blood away under high pressure; veins return blood under low pressure and contain valves to prevent backflow.

Path of Blood (Human): Right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary semilunar valve → pulmonary arteries (lungs) → pulmonary veins → left atrium → bicuspid (mitral) valve → left ventricle → aortic semilunar valve → aorta → systemic circuit.

Heartbeat Control: Sinoatrial (SA) node acts as the pacemaker to initiate electrical signals; Atrioventricular (AV) node delays and transmits signals to the ventricles to coordinate contraction (systole = contraction, diastole = relaxation).

ECG Waves: P wave represents atrial depolarization (about to contract); QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization (about to contract, atria relaxing); T wave represents ventricular repolarization (recovery).
7.memory_anchor:
Heart Valve Position Mnemonic

Remember: Try before you Buy

  • Tricuspid valve is on the Right side of the heart.
  • Bicuspid (mitral) valve is on the Left side of the heart.

flashcards.q: Trace the pathway of a red blood cell from the systemic tissues back to the systemic tissues in a human.
flashcards.a: Systemic tissues -> Venae cavae -> Right atrium -> Tricuspid valve -> Right ventricle -> Pulmonary semilunar valve -> Pulmonary trunk/arteries -> Lungs (oxygenation) -> Pulmonary veins -> Left atrium -> Bicuspid (mitral) valve -> Left ventricle -> Aortic semilunar valve -> Aorta -> Systemic arteries/tissues.

flashcards.q: What are the events corresponding to the P, QRS, and T waves of an electrocardiogram (ECG)?
flashcards.a: The P wave represents atrial depolarization (atria about to contract, triggered by the SA node); the QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization (ventricles about to contract) and hides atrial repolarization; the T wave represents ventricular repolarization (ventricular recovery).

flashcards.q: Explain how blood is returned to the heart in low-pressure veins against gravity.
flashcards.a: Venous return is driven by skeletal muscle contraction (which squeezes the veins and pushes blood forward), one-way valves (which prevent backflow), and a respiratory pump (which decreases thoracic pressure during inspiration, pulling blood into the chest cavity).

7.outline_blanks: The mammalian heart features a double-loop pathway. Deoxygenated blood enters the [[right atrium]] via the venae cavae, passes through the [[tricuspid]] valve, and is pumped to the lungs, while oxygenated blood is pumped by the thick-walled [[left ventricle]] into the [[aorta]]. Heart rhythm is coordinated by the [[sinoatrial node]] pacemaker.

7.title: Respiratory System
cheat_card: Respiration involves three exchange steps: ventilation (breathing), external respiration (gas exchange between air and blood in lungs), and internal respiration (gas exchange between blood and tissue fluids).

Fish utilize highly efficient countercurrent exchange in gills: water flows opposite to the direction of oxygen-depleted blood, maintaining a concentration gradient that extracts up to 90% of dissolved oxygen.
Insects bypass blood-mediated transport entirely using a tracheal system (tracheae → tubules → tracheoles) that delivers air directly to cells. Air sacs act like bellows.

Mammalian breathing uses negative pressure: inspiration occurs when the diaphragm contracts and lowers (thoracic pressure drops below atmospheric), while expiration occurs when the diaphragm relaxes and rises (thoracic pressure rises, forcing air out).
7.memory_anchor:
Respiration Exchange Efficiency Comparison

  • Fish Gills: Countercurrent Flow (Water and blood flow in opposite directions, maintaining a diffusion gradient along the entire length of the capillary; extracts ~90% oxygen).
  • Mammalian Lungs: Tidal Ventilation (In/out same path; fresh and residual air mix, decreasing efficiency).
  • Bird Lungs: One-Way Flow (Air sacs act as reservoirs; fresh air flows continuously through parabronchi in one direction, preventing mixing; highest efficiency).

flashcards.q: Explain why countercurrent exchange in fish gills is more efficient than concurrent exchange.
flashcards.a: In countercurrent exchange, water and blood flow in opposite directions. This ensures that oxygen-poor blood constantly encounters water with a higher oxygen concentration, maintaining a diffusion gradient along the entire capillary bed. Concurrent flow would cause blood and water to reach an equilibrium, stopping diffusion halfway.

flashcards.q: Describe the mechanical events that cause inspiration and expiration in mammals.
flashcards.a: Inspiration occurs when the rib cage is elevated and the diaphragm contracts and flattens. This increases thoracic cavity volume and decreases internal pressure below atmospheric pressure, sucking air in. Expiration occurs when the diaphragm relaxes and rises, and the rib cage lowers, decreasing volume and increasing thoracic pressure, forcing air out.

flashcards.q: Compare tidal ventilation in mammals with the respiratory system of birds.
flashcards.a: Mammals use tidal ventilation, meaning air enters and exits the same way, mixing fresh air with stale residual air. Birds have a highly efficient one-way ventilation system using anterior and posterior air sacs. Fresh air flows continuously through the lungs in one direction, never mixing with used air.

7.outline_blanks: Gas exchange occurs via diffusion across thin surfaces. Fish maximize extraction using [[countercurrent exchange]] across gills, whereas insects deliver air directly to cells using a [[tracheal system]]. Mammalian inspiration is driven by a [[negative pressure]] created when the diaphragm [[contracts and lowers]].

7.title: Nervous System
cheat_card: Neurons consist of a cell body, dendrites (receive inputs), and an axon (conducts impulses). Myelinated axons conduct impulses rapidly via saltatory (jumping) conduction between nodes.
Resting Membrane Potential: Set at -70 mV (inside negative) by the active Na+/K+ ATPase pump (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in) and maintained by passive diffusion of K+ out through K+ leak channels.

Action Potential: Depolarization to threshold (-55 mV) opens gated Na+ channels (Na+ enters, depolarizing to +40 mV). At peak, Na+ channels inactivate and gated K+ channels open (K+ exits, repolarizing). A refractory period prevents back-propagation.

Synaptic Transmission: Action potential reaches terminal → opens gated calcium (Ca2+) channels → calcium influx triggers neurotransmitter exocytosis into the synaptic cleft → neurotransmitters bind postsynaptic receptors.

Autonomic Divisions: Sympathetic coordinates fight-or-flight stress responses (uses norepinephrine, increases heart rate/bronchiodilation); Parasympathetic coordinates rest-and-digest (uses acetylcholine, slows heart/promotes digestion).
7.memory_anchor:
Salty Banana Memory Hook

For resting potentials, remember a Salty Banana:

  • Salty (Sodium / Na+) is high on the outside (ocean is salty).
  • Banana (Potassium / K+) is high on the inside (bananas are rich in potassium).
  • The active Na+/K+ pump maintains this by pumping 3 Na+ OUT and 2 K+ IN.

flashcards.q: Explain how the resting membrane potential is generated and maintained in a neuron.
flashcards.a: The resting potential (approx. -70 mV) is established by the active Na+/K+ ATPase pump, which uses ATP to pump 3 Na+ out of the cell for every 2 K+ pumped in. It is maintained by open potassium leak channels, which allow K+ to diffuse passively down its concentration gradient out of the cell, leaving a net negative charge inside.

flashcards.q: Trace the sequence of events during a synaptic transmission from the presynaptic neuron to the postsynaptic neuron.
flashcards.a: When an action potential reaches the axon terminal, it opens voltage-gated calcium channels. The resulting influx of calcium (Ca2+) triggers synaptic vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release neurotransmitters via exocytosis. The neurotransmitters diffuse across the synaptic cleft and bind to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, altering its potential.

flashcards.q: Contrast the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions of the autonomic nervous system.
flashcards.a: The sympathetic division coordinates 'fight-or-flight' stress responses, accelerating heart rate, dilating bronchi, and using norepinephrine as its primary neurotransmitter. The parasympathetic division coordinates 'rest-and-digest' responses, slowing heart rate, promoting digestion, and using acetylcholine as its primary neurotransmitter.

7.outline_blanks: The resting potential of a neuron is established by the [[Na+/K+ ATPase pump]] which pumps sodium out and potassium in. An action potential is triggered when depolarization reaches the [[threshold]], causing [[voltage-gated Na+ channels]] to open. Synaptic transmission relies on a calcium influx causing the exocytosis of [[neurotransmitters]] into the cleft.

7.title: Sense Receptors
cheat_card: Receptors perform sensory transduction, converting stimuli to nerve impulses. Types include chemoreceptors (taste/smell), photoreceptors (rods/cones), mechanoreceptors (pressure/sound/balance), thermoreceptors (temp), and nociceptors (pain).

Human Eye: Outer sclera becomes the transparent cornea. Middle choroid forms the ciliary body (controls lens shape during visual accommodation) and the iris (controls pupil size). Inner retina contains rods (low light, rhodopsin) and cones (bright light, B/G/R color). Cones are packed in the fovea centralis.
Human Ear: Sound vibrates the tympanic membrane, transferring pressure to ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) which multiply pressure. Stapes strikes the oval window, vibrating fluid in the cochlea.

Hearing & Equilibrium: Cochlear sound waves vibrate the basilar membrane in the organ of Corti, bending the stereocilia on hair cells. Equilibrium is sensed by hair cells in semicircular canals (rotational) and the utricle and saccule (gravitational).
7.memory_anchor:
Retinal Integration and Synaptic Convergence

  • Photoreceptors (Rods/Cones) → [Synapse with] → Bipolar Cells → [Synapse with] → Ganglion Cells (Axons form the Optic Nerve).
  • Sharpness Hook: Cones have low convergence (few cones per ganglion cell), providing high-acuity central vision in the fovea centralis. Rods have high convergence (many rods per ganglion cell), giving high sensitivity for low-light but low detail.

flashcards.q: Explain how the human eye adjusts its focus for near versus distant objects.
flashcards.a: The eye undergoes visual accommodation via the ciliary muscle which controls the shape of the lens. To view a distant object, the ciliary muscle relaxes, causing the lens to flatten. To view a near object, the ciliary muscle contracts, causing the lens to become more rounded and thick, increasing its refractive power.

flashcards.q: Describe the path of sound waves and pressure through the human ear to the generation of a nerve impulse.
flashcards.a: Sound waves enter the auditory canal -> vibrate the tympanic membrane -> pass through the ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) which multiply pressure -> stapes strikes the oval window -> pressure waves travel through fluid in the cochlea -> vibrate the basilar membrane in the organ of Corti -> bend the stereocilia on hair cells (mechanoreceptors) -> generate action potentials in the cochlear nerve.

flashcards.q: How does the inner ear detect rotational and gravitational equilibrium?
flashcards.a: Rotational equilibrium is detected by hair cells in the ampullae of the semicircular canals, which bend when fluid shifts during rotation. Gravitational equilibrium is detected by hair cells in the utricle and saccule, which shift in response to the pull of gravity when the head bends.

7.outline_blanks: The process of converting environmental stimuli into nerve impulses is called [[sensory transduction]]. In the eye, light is focused on the [[fovea centralis]] of the retina, which is packed with color-detecting [[cone cells]]. In the ear, sound waves vibrate the [[basilar membrane]], bending the stereocilia of hair cells.

7.title: Muscle Contraction
cheat_card: Muscular tissue contains contractile actin (thin) and myosin (thick) filaments. Skeletal muscle is voluntary and striated; smooth muscle is involuntary and non-striated; cardiac muscle is striated, involuntary, and joined by intercalated disks.

Neuromuscular Junction: Action potential at motor neuron axon terminal triggers calcium influx → exocytosis of acetylcholine (ACh) → binds sarcolemma receptors → propagates action potential down T-tubules.
Sarcoplasmic Reticulum (SR): Action potential in T-tubules activates receptors to open calcium release channels, releasing stored calcium (Ca2+) into the sarcoplasm.

Sliding Filament Theory: Calcium binds to troponin, which shifts tropomyosin to uncover myosin-binding sites on actin. Myosin heads form cross-bridges with actin, perform a power stroke (releasing ADP/Pi), bind ATP to detach, and hydrolyze it to cock back for another cycle.
7.memory_anchor:
Skeletal Muscle Contraction Flow

  1. ACh Release at Neuromuscular Junction → Muscle Action Potential.
  2. Action Potential travels down T-tubules → Calcium release from Sarcoplasmic Reticulum.
  3. Calcium binds Troponin → Tropomyosin shifts → Actin active sites exposed.
  4. Cross-bridges form (Myosin binds Actin) → Power stroke slides filaments → Sarcomere contracts.

flashcards.q: How does a neuronal impulse trigger the release of calcium within a muscle cell?
flashcards.a: The action potential reaches the neuromuscular junction, triggering the exocytosis of acetylcholine (ACh). ACh binds to receptors on the muscle sarcolemma, generating a muscle action potential. This potential propagates down the T-tubules, activating voltage-sensitive receptors that open calcium release channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum, releasing calcium into the sarcoplasm.

flashcards.q: Describe the roles of troponin and tropomyosin in regulating muscle contraction.
flashcards.a: In relaxed muscle, tropomyosin covers the myosin-binding sites on actin, blocking cross-bridge formation. When calcium is released, it binds to troponin, causing a conformational change that pulls tropomyosin away from the active sites. This exposes the binding sites, allowing myosin heads to bind to actin.

flashcards.q: Outline the steps of the cross-bridge cycle (sliding filament theory) during contraction.
flashcards.a: 1) Myosin heads bind to the exposed active sites on actin to form cross-bridges. 2) The power stroke occurs as ADP and inorganic phosphate are released, causing the myosin head to bend and pull the actin filament inward. 3) ATP binds to the myosin head, causing it to detach from actin. 4) ATP hydrolysis (ATP -> ADP + Pi) cock-charges the myosin head back into its high-energy state.

7.outline_blanks: Muscle contraction is initiated when an action potential travels down [[T-tubules]] to trigger calcium release from the [[sarcoplasmic reticulum]]. Calcium binds to [[troponin]], which shifts [[tropomyosin]] to expose active sites on actin. Myosin heads then form [[cross-bridges]] and perform a power stroke to contract.

8.title: Nature/Nurture
cheat_card: Most animal behaviors have a genetic basis (nature) but are modulated by environmental influences (nurture), linked to the nervous and endocrine systems.

Nest-building in lovebirds demonstrates genetic control: Fischer's lovebirds carry material in their beaks, peach-faced lovebirds tuck strips in feathers, and their hybrids show intermediate, confused behaviors.
Garter snake food choice is genetically wired: inland populations eat fish/frogs and refuse slugs, coastal populations eat slugs, and their hybrids accept slugs.
Human twin studies (e.g., Scott & Mark Kelly) show twins separated at birth share similar food preferences, activity levels, and mate selection.
Maternal nurturing behavior in mice post-birth depends on the expression of a single gene called fosB; mutating it leads to pup neglect.
8.memory_anchor: Genetics of Behavior: Lovebirds (beak vs feather nesting hybrids), Garter Snakes (inland refuse vs coastal accept slug hybrids), Mice (fosB gene deletion causes maternal neglect).

flashcards.q: What experimental evidence from lovebird hybrid breeding supports the idea that behavior has a genetic basis?
flashcards.a: Fischer lovebirds carry nesting material in their beaks, while peach-faced lovebirds tuck it into their feathers. Hybrid offspring attempt both methods and exhibit extreme difficulty carrying materials, proving nest-building behavior is genetically inherited.

flashcards.q: How does the diet of coastal and inland garter snakes, along with their hybrids, demonstrate the genetic basis of behavior?
flashcards.a: Inland snakes feed on frogs and fish and refuse slugs, while coastal snakes feed on slugs. Hybrid offspring accept slugs as a food source, indicating that slug preference is a genetically controlled trait.

flashcards.q: What genetic factor determines post-birth maternal nurturing behavior in mice, and what happens when it is mutated?
flashcards.a: Maternal nurturing behavior is dependent on the presence of a single gene termed fosB. When both copies of the fosB gene are inactive, the mother mouse neglects her pups, failing to retrieve or warm them.

8.outline_blanks: Experiments with lovebirds, garter snakes, and mice show that behavior has a genetic basis. For example, nest-building hybrids of Fischer and peach-faced lovebirds show confusion, and maternal care in mice depends on a single gene named [[fosB]]. Similarly, coastal garter snakes accept [[slugs]] as food, whereas inland snakes refuse them, with hybrids showing intermediate acceptance.

8.title: Conditioning
cheat_card: Associative learning involves a change in behavior through linking two events, split into classical and operant conditioning.
Classical conditioning pairs two different types of stimuli to elicit an involuntary response (e.g., Pavlov's dogs salivating to a bell associated with food).
Operant conditioning strengthens stimulus-response connections through trial and reinforcement/reward (e.g., animal trick-training).
Imprinting occurs when an animal mimics a behavior during a highly sensitive, restrictive sensitive period right after birth.
Insight learning is solving a novel problem without prior experience by drawing on past experiences in other contexts.
8.memory_anchor:
Conditioning Types:
- Classical = Stimulus-Stimulus (Pavlov's bell + food = saliva)
- Operant = Stimulus-Response (Trick + Reward = behavior strengthened)
- Insight = Sudden solution (No trial-and-error)

flashcards.q: How does classical conditioning differ from operant conditioning in terms of stimuli and responses?
flashcards.a: Classical conditioning pairs two different stimuli to elicit an involuntary, automatic response (like Pavlov's dogs salivating at a bell), whereas operant conditioning strengthens a voluntary behavior through rewards or reinforcement.

flashcards.q: What is the biological term for a durable change in behavior brought about by experience, and what is a sensitive period?
flashcards.a: A durable change in behavior brought about by experience is called learning. A sensitive period is a defined window of time during development when a specific behavior (like imprinting) must be learned.

flashcards.q: What is insight learning and how does it differ from trial-and-error learning?
flashcards.a: Insight learning is solving a problem without prior direct experience, where the animal draws upon prior experiences from different circumstances to formulate a new solution, rather than slowly establishing stimulus-response connections.

8.outline_blanks: Associative learning can occur via [[classical conditioning]], where two different stimuli are paired (like Pavlov's dogs salivating at a bell), or [[operant conditioning]], which strengthens stimulus-response connections through trial and reward. In contrast, [[insight learning]] allows an animal to solve a new problem without prior experience by drawing on past memories.

8.title: Repro strategies
cheat_card: In polygamous systems, one male mates with multiple females, with females investing more energy in offspring care.
In polyandrous systems, one female mates with multiple males; this is favored when the environment cannot support young without multiple male helpers.
In monogamous systems, one male mates with one female, favored when mating opportunities are limited, territoriality exists, and paternal certainty is high.
Sexual selection drives adaptive changes in males and females leading to female choice (selecting traits) and male competition (combating for access).
8.memory_anchor:
Mating Systems:
- Poly-gamy: 1 male, many females. High female investment.
- Poly-andry: 1 female, many males. Harsh environment needs multiple dads.
- Mono-gamy: 1 male, 1 female. Paternal certainty & shared defense.

flashcards.q: Under what environmental and reproductive conditions is monogamy favored in animal species?
flashcards.a: Monogamy is favored when males have limited mating opportunities, territoriality exists, and there is high paternal certainty (meaning the male is certain the offspring are his), making shared parental care adaptive.

flashcards.q: What characterizes a polyandrous mating system and when does it typically occur?
flashcards.a: Polyandrous systems involve one female mating with multiple males. This typically occurs in environments that cannot support young without the active, cooperative parenting support of multiple males.

flashcards.q: What are the two primary outcomes of sexual selection that lead to differential reproductive success?
flashcards.a: The two outcomes are female choice (where females select males based on specific traits/behaviors) and male competition (where males compete directly, e.g., through threat postures or fighting, for access to females).

8.outline_blanks: Different reproductive strategies exist: in [[polygamous]] systems, one male mates with multiple females who invest more in care, whereas in [[polyandrous]] systems, one female mates with multiple males to cope with harsh environments. Under conditions of high paternal certainty and limited mates, [[monogamous]] pairings are favored to maximize reproductive success.

8.title: Energy flow
cheat_card: Energy flows in a one-way direction through ecosystems from autotrophs (producers) to heterotrophs (consumers).
The 10% rule states that only about 10% of energy is transferred to the next trophic level, while 90% is lost as heat, following the Laws of Thermodynamics.
Grazing food webs start with living autotrophs; detrital food webs begin with decomposers and detritus.
Biomass is the number of organisms at each level multiplied by their weight.
Unlike energy, toxic pollutants undergo biomagnification, becoming increasingly concentrated at higher trophic levels.
8.memory_anchor:
Energy vs. Toxins:
- Energy DECREASES up the pyramid (10% rule, 90% lost as heat).
- Toxins INCREASE up the pyramid (Biomagnification in fat tissue).

flashcards.q: Why is energy flow through an ecosystem considered a one-way path, and what happens to the energy that is not transferred?
flashcards.a: Energy flow is one-way because energy enters as solar radiation, gets captured by producers, and is passed up trophic levels. Energy not transferred (roughly 90%) is lost to the environment as heat, satisfying the Laws of Thermodynamics.

flashcards.q: Contrast the starting points of a grazing food web versus a detrital food web.
flashcards.a: A grazing food web begins with living autotrophs (photoautotrophs/producers), whereas a detrital food web begins with detritus (dead organic matter) and decomposers/detritivores.

flashcards.q: How does biomagnification differ from the normal pattern of energy transfer in an ecological pyramid?
flashcards.a: While energy decreases by approximately 90% at each step up the ecological pyramid, persistent chemical pollutants are not broken down or excreted, resulting in their concentration increasing (biomagnification) at higher trophic levels.

8.outline_blanks: Energy enters ecosystems through producers and moves up trophic levels, but only about [[10%]] of energy is transferred to the next level, with the rest lost as [[heat]]. In contrast to energy loss, toxic pollutants undergo [[biomagnification]], which causes them to become more concentrated in apex predators.

8.title: Biomes
cheat_card: Biomes are major terrestrial ecosystems characterized by temperature and precipitation, changing with latitude and altitude.
The tundra covers 20% of Earth's land surface, characterized by a permanently frozen permafrost layer that prevents tree root growth.
Taiga (coniferous forest) features cone-bearing trees with needles adapted to cold, whereas temperate deciduous forests have four distinct seasons and abundant ground-life.
Tropical rainforests feature high rain/warmth, vertical layering (understory, canopy), epiphytes, and nutrient-poor soil due to rapid nutrient recycling.
Deserts occur at 30° latitude with <25 cm rainfall; shrublands (chaparral) have dry summers/wet winters and are highly flammable.
8.memory_anchor:
Biome Quick Guide:
- Tundra: Permafrost, no trees
- Taiga: Needle leaves, cone trees
- Deciduous: 4 seasons, rich ground-life
- Tropical: Canopy, nutrient-poor soil, epiphytes
- Shrubland: Chaparral, flammable
- Desert: <25cm rain, 30 degrees latitude

flashcards.q: Why are trees absent in the tundra biome, and what percentage of Earth's land surface does it cover?
flashcards.a: The tundra covers 20% of Earth's land surface. Trees cannot grow there because the growing season is too short, roots cannot penetrate the permanently frozen permafrost layer, and the shallow, boggy soil does not support anchoring.

flashcards.q: Why are tropical rainforest soils nutrient-poor despite the biome's high biodiversity and plant density?
flashcards.a: The soils are nutrient-poor because the warm temperatures and high moisture levels cause extremely rapid decomposition and immediate re-absorption of nutrients by plants, leaving little organic matter in the soil.

flashcards.q: Compare the climate characteristics of chaparral (shrublands) and deserts.
flashcards.a: Chaparral has dry summers and wet winters with highly flammable shrubs. Deserts have annual rainfall under 25 cm, large temperature variations between day and night, and occur around 30° latitude due to descending dry air currents.

8.outline_blanks: Terrestrial biomes are defined by temperature and precipitation. The tundra is characterized by a permanently frozen [[permafrost]] layer that prevents tree growth, while tropical rainforests feature complex vertical structures and [[nutrient-poor]] soils. Temperate deciduous forests experience [[four]] distinct seasons and support diverse ground-life.

8.title: Aquatic zones
cheat_card: Lake zones are classified as littoral (near shore), limnetic (sunlit open water), profundal (dark), and benthic (lake bottom).
Deep temperate lakes stratify in summer into the epilimnion (warm surface), thermocline (middle), and hypolimnion (cold bottom), mixing during fall/spring overturns.
Estuaries are highly productive mixing zones of fresh and saltwater, supporting development of two-thirds of marine fish/shellfish.
Ocean pelagic zones include epipelagic (nutrient-poor), mesopelagic (sunlit/high life), and bathypelagic (complete darkness, bioluminescence).
The abyssal plain is extreme cold/high pressure, relying on organic debris and hydrothermal vents where chemoautotrophs utilize hydrogen sulfide at 350°C.
8.memory_anchor:
Vertical Water Profile:
- Lake: Epilimnion (Warm Surface) -> Thermocline (Rapid Drop) -> Hypolimnion (Cold Bottom)
- Ocean Vents: 350°C water releases Hydrogen Sulfide (H2S) for chemoautotrophy.

flashcards.q: Describe the three temperature layers that form in deep temperate lakes during summer stratification.
flashcards.a: The three layers are the epilimnion (warm, sunlit surface layer), the thermocline (middle layer where temperature drops rapidly), and the hypolimnion (cold, dense bottom layer).

flashcards.q: Why are estuaries ecologically and economically critical for marine fisheries?
flashcards.a: Estuaries are regions where fresh water and seawater mix. They are highly productive, nutrient-rich environments that support the developmental stages of nearly two-thirds of all marine fishes and shellfish.

flashcards.q: What is the chemical source of energy for ecosystems near hydrothermal vents on the abyssal plain, and how is it generated?
flashcards.a: The energy source is hydrogen sulfide (H2S). It is generated when seawater percolates through cracks in the ocean floor and is heated to 350°C, causing sulfate to react with water. Chemoautotrophs use it to produce organic nutrients.

8.outline_blanks: Lakes stratify in the summer into a warm surface [[epilimnion]] and a cold bottom [[hypolimnion]], which mix during seasonal overturns. Marine ecosystems feature a sunlit [[euphotic]] zone and a deep abyssal plain where chemoautotrophic organisms utilize [[hydrogen sulfide]] released from hydrothermal vents.

8.title: Conservation
cheat_card: Biodiversity includes genetic diversity (variation in a population), community diversity (species interactions), and landscape diversity (ecosystem networks).
Biodiversity hotspots contain 44% of higher plants and 35% of terrestrial vertebrates in only 1.4% of Earth's land area.
Major causes of extinction are habitat loss (85%), exotic species (50%), pollution (24%), and overexploitation (17%).

Key conservation terms include keystone species (essential for community viability), flagstone species (charismatic species eliciting human emotion), and the edge effect (adverse boundary conditions in fragmented habitats).
Principles of restoration ecology: begin ASAP, use biological techniques to mimic natural processes, and target sustainable development.
8.memory_anchor:
Extinction Threats (H.E.P.O.D.):
- Habitat Loss: 85%
- Exotic Species: 50%
- Pollution: 24%
- Overexploitation: 17%
- Disease: 3%

flashcards.q: Compare genetic, community (ecosystem), and landscape diversity as levels of biodiversity.
flashcards.a: Genetic diversity is the variation within a single population; community diversity depends on interactions between different species in an area; landscape diversity involves multiple interacting ecosystems within a region, threatened by fragmentation.

flashcards.q: What are the percentage impacts of the four major causes of extinction listed in conservation biology?
flashcards.a: The major causes and percentages of species affected are habitat loss (85%), exotic species (50%), pollution (24%), and overexploitation (17%).

flashcards.q: What are the three core principles of restoration ecology?
flashcards.a: The three principles are: (1) begin restoration as soon as possible before fragments are lost, (2) understand natural history to use biological techniques that mimic natural processes, and (3) aim for sustainable development.

8.outline_blanks: Biodiversity conservation is prioritized at genetic, community, and landscape levels, with [[habitat loss]] being the leading cause of extinction at 85%. Techniques focus on preserving [[keystone]] species that maintain community structure, avoiding fragmentation that exacerbates the [[edge effect]], and restoring habitats using sustainable principles.

8.title: Light systems
cheat_card: Photosynthetic pigments absorb visible light; chlorophyll absorbs red and blue wavelengths and reflects green.
Light-dependent reactions occur in the thylakoid membrane, using pigment-collecting complexes called photosystems (PS II and PS I).
The noncyclic pathway flows from PS II to PS I, generating both ATP (via chemiosmosis) and NADPH.
In PS II, light energy ejects electrons from the reaction center (chlorophyll a), which are replaced by splitting water ($H_2O$), releasing oxygen gas.
The cyclic pathway recirculates electrons through PS I to produce only ATP (no NADPH).
8.memory_anchor:
Noncyclic Pathway Flow:
Light -> PS II (Water splits to release O2) -> ETC pumps H+ -> PS I (e- ejected to NADP+ Reductase) -> NADPH.

flashcards.q: Why does chlorophyll appear green to our eyes, and what wavelengths of light does it primarily absorb?
flashcards.a: Chlorophyll appears green because it reflects and transmits green light wavelengths. It primarily absorbs the blue and red regions of the visible light spectrum to drive photosynthesis.

flashcards.q: What are the product differences between the noncyclic and cyclic electron pathways in the light-dependent reactions?
flashcards.a: The noncyclic pathway utilizes both PS II and PS I to produce both ATP and NADPH, whereas the cyclic pathway recirculates electrons through PS I and produces only ATP.

flashcards.q: How are the electrons lost from the reaction center of Photosystem II replaced during the noncyclic pathway?
flashcards.a: The lost electrons are replaced by splitting a water molecule (H2O), which yields electrons, releases oxygen gas (O2), and contributes hydrogen ions (H+) to the thylakoid space.

8.outline_blanks: Photosynthesis begins as pigments in the thylakoid membrane absorb solar energy. In the noncyclic pathway, [[PS II]] absorbs light and ejects electrons, which are replaced by splitting [[water]]. These electrons flow down an electron transport chain to [[PS I]], which ultimately reduces NADP+ to [[NADPH]].

8.title: Light dependent/independent
cheat_card: Light-dependent reactions occur in the thylakoids, converting light and water into ATP and NADPH while releasing oxygen.
Light-independent reactions (Calvin Cycle) occur in the stroma, utilizing ATP and NADPH to reduce $CO_2$ to a carbohydrate.
The Calvin Cycle has three phases: $CO_2$ fixation, $CO_2$ reduction, and RuBP regeneration.
$CO_2$ fixation is catalyzed by Rubisco, attaching $CO_2$ to the 5-carbon RuBP, which splits into two 3-carbon 3PG molecules.
For every three turns of the Calvin Cycle, five G3P are recycled into three RuBP, with one G3P exiting the cycle.
8.memory_anchor:
Calvin Cycle Math:
3 CO2 + 3 RuBP (5C) = 6 3PG (3C)
6 3PG + 6 ATP + 6 NADPH = 6 G3P (3C)
5 G3P (15C) + 3 ATP = 3 RuBP (15C) [Regeneration]
1 Net G3P exits to make glucose (requires 6 turns total).

flashcards.q: Compare the cellular location and primary inputs/outputs of the light-dependent reactions and the Calvin Cycle.
flashcards.a: Light-dependent reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes, inputting light and water to output ATP, NADPH, and oxygen. The Calvin Cycle occurs in the stroma, inputting carbon dioxide, ATP, and NADPH to output G3P (carbohydrates).

flashcards.q: What role does the enzyme Rubisco play in carbon fixation, and what is its abundance in the chloroplast?
flashcards.a: Rubisco (RuBP carboxylase) catalyzes the attachment of carbon dioxide to the 5-carbon molecule RuBP. It is highly abundant, making up 20% to 50% of all chloroplast protein.

flashcards.q: Explain the mathematical recycling of G3P to RuBP in the regeneration phase of the Calvin Cycle.
flashcards.a: To keep the cycle running, for every 3 turns of the Calvin Cycle, 5 molecules of G3P (each with 3 carbons, totaling 15 carbons) are converted using ATP into 3 molecules of RuBP (each with 5 carbons, totaling 15 carbons).

8.outline_blanks: The light reactions occur in the thylakoids and generate ATP and NADPH, which are then used in the stroma during the [[Calvin Cycle]]. The first step of this light-independent process is carbon fixation, where CO2 is attached to RuBP by the enzyme [[Rubisco]]. The resulting molecules are reduced to G3P, with five of these molecules recycled to regenerate [[three]] molecules of RuBP.

8.title: Photosynthesis reactants
cheat_card: The overall raw materials for photosynthesis are carbon dioxide ($CO_2$) and water ($H_2O$).
Water is absorbed by roots and travels up vascular tissue; $CO_2$ enters the leaf through small openings called stomata.
During the light reactions, water is oxidized (split) to yield electrons, $H^+$ ions, and oxygen gas ($O_2$) as a byproduct.
In the stroma, $CO_2$ is combined with hydrogen atoms carried by the coenzyme NADPH to synthesize glucose ($C_6H_{12}O_6$).
8.memory_anchor:
Photosynthesis Formula:
6 CO2 (enters via stomata) + 6 H2O (via roots/vascular) + Light -> C6H12O6 (in stroma) + 6 O2 (released from split H2O)

flashcards.q: How do carbon dioxide and water enter a plant and reach the site of photosynthesis?
flashcards.a: Water is absorbed by roots and transported upward through vascular tissue to the leaves. Carbon dioxide enters the leaves from the atmosphere through small openings called stomata and diffuses into the chloroplasts.

flashcards.q: What coenzyme acts as the hydrogen/electron carrier in photosynthesis, and what are its oxidized and reduced states?
flashcards.a: The coenzyme is NADP+. Its oxidized state is NADP+, and its reduced state is NADPH (formed when it accepts 2 electrons and 1 hydrogen ion).

flashcards.q: What is the fate of the oxygen atoms in water during the light reactions of photosynthesis?
flashcards.a: The water molecules are split (oxidized) at Photosystem II, and the oxygen atoms combine to form oxygen gas (O2), which is released into the atmosphere through the stomata.

8.outline_blanks: Photosynthesis utilizes light energy to transform carbon dioxide and water into carbohydrates. Water enters via roots and moves up vascular tissue, whereas carbon dioxide enters the leaf through openings called [[stomata]]. During the light reactions, water is split to release [[oxygen]] gas, and its electrons reduce the coenzyme [[NADP+]] to NADPH.

8.title: Plant strategies
cheat_card: In hot, dry climates, stomata close to prevent water loss, causing $CO_2$ levels to drop and $O_2$ to rise, triggering wasteful photorespiration.
C4 plants bypass photorespiration by fixing $CO_2$ to PEP (phosphoenolpyruvate) to form a 4-carbon molecule, separating fixation spatially.
CAM plants partition carbon fixation by time: they open stomata at night to store $CO_2$ in vacuoles, keeping stomata closed during daylight.
C4 plants (e.g., corn, sugarcane) have 2-3x higher productivity in hot, dry climates, but C3 plants are better adapted to cool climates below 25°C.
8.memory_anchor:
Avoiding Photorespiration:
- C4: Spatial separation (PEP carboxylase in mesophyll, Calvin Cycle in bundle sheath).
- CAM: Temporal separation (Open stomata at night, Calvin Cycle during day).

flashcards.q: What is photorespiration, and why is it disadvantageous for C3 plants in hot, dry climates?
flashcards.a: Photorespiration is a wasteful process that occurs when closed stomata cause CO2 levels to drop and O2 levels to rise inside the leaf. Rubisco binds O2 instead of CO2, releasing CO2 and consuming energy without producing carbohydrates.

flashcards.q: Explain how CAM plants conserve water while still performing photosynthesis.
flashcards.a: CAM plants open their stomata at night to capture CO2 and store it as C4 molecules in vacuoles. During the day, they close their stomata to prevent water loss and release the stored CO2 to the Calvin cycle using light energy.

flashcards.q: Give three examples of C4 plants and specify the temperature threshold below which C3 plants are better adapted.
flashcards.a: Examples of C4 plants include corn, sugarcane, Bermuda grass, and crab grass. C3 plants are better adapted to cool, moist environments below 25°C.

8.outline_blanks: Under hot and dry conditions, C3 plants close their stomata, resulting in wasteful [[photorespiration]]. C4 plants bypass this by fixing CO2 to PEP, producing a 4-carbon molecule. In contrast, CAM plants conserve water by opening stomata at [[night]] to store carbon in vacuoles, then release it during the [[day]] to run the Calvin cycle.

8.title: Cell respiration stages
cheat_card: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm anaerobically, splitting glucose to 2 pyruvates, producing a net of 2 ATP and 2 NADH.
The preparatory reaction occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, converting pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and releasing 2 $CO_2$.
The citric acid cycle in the matrix combines acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate to form citric acid, yielding 2 ATP, 6 NADH, 2 FADH2, and 4 $CO_2$ per glucose.
The ETC in the cristae uses oxidative phosphorylation (chemiosmosis) to generate 32 or 34 ATP, with oxygen as the final acceptor.
Overall aerobic cellular respiration yields a net of 36-38 ATP per glucose molecule.
8.memory_anchor:
Cell Respiration Stage Map:
1. Glycolysis (Cytoplasm, Anaerobic, Net 2 ATP)
2. Prep Reaction (Matrix, Aerobic, 0 ATP, 2 CO2)
3. Citric Acid Cycle (Matrix, Aerobic, 2 ATP, 4 CO2)
4. ETC (Cristae, Aerobic, 32 or 34 ATP, 6 H2O)

flashcards.q: State the location, oxygen requirement, and net ATP yield of glycolysis.
flashcards.a: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm, is anaerobic (does not require oxygen), and produces a net gain of 2 ATP molecules per glucose.

flashcards.q: Detail the inputs and outputs of the preparatory reaction per molecule of glucose.
flashcards.a: For each glucose (2 pyruvates), the prep reaction takes in 2 pyruvates and 2 Coenzyme A, producing 2 acetyl-CoA, 2 NADH, and releasing 2 CO2 as waste. No ATP is produced.

flashcards.q: What molecule begins the citric acid cycle by combining with the incoming acetyl group, what molecule is formed, and where does this occur?
flashcards.a: The 2-carbon acetyl group from acetyl-CoA combines with the 4-carbon molecule oxaloacetate to form the 6-carbon molecule citric acid (citrate) in the mitochondrial matrix.

8.outline_blanks: Cellular respiration consists of four distinct phases. Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm, converting glucose into pyruvate. Pyruvate then enters the mitochondrial matrix for the preparatory reaction to form [[acetyl-CoA]], which is oxidized in the [[citric acid cycle]] to produce NADH and FADH2. Finally, these coenzymes deliver electrons to the ETC located on the [[cristae]] to synthesize ATP.

8.title: ETC role
cheat_card: The ETC is located in the mitochondrial cristae in eukaryotes and the plasma membrane in aerobic prokaryotes.
Electrons from NADH and FADH2 flow down a series of carriers, including cytochromes (proteins with central iron-containing heme groups).
Oxygen serves as the final electron acceptor, combining with $H^+$ to form water ($H_2O$).
Hydrogens from NADH deliver energy to yield 3 ATP, while those from FADH2 yield 2 ATP.
Without oxygen, coenzymes cannot be recycled back to $NAD^+$ and $FAD$, bringing aerobic respiration to a halt.
8.memory_anchor:
ETC Carriers:
NADH -> Complex I -> 3 ATP
FADH2 -> Complex II -> 2 ATP
Cytochromes (Heme/Iron) -> Oxygen (Final Acceptor) -> H2O

flashcards.q: What are cytochromes, and where are they located within eukaryotic cells?
flashcards.a: Cytochromes are electron carrier proteins containing heme groups with central iron atoms. They form part of the electron transport chain located in the cristae (inner membrane) of the mitochondria.

flashcards.q: Explain why oxygen is crucial for the continuous recycling of NAD+ and FAD coenzymes in cellular respiration.
flashcards.a: Oxygen acts as the final electron acceptor at the end of the ETC. Without oxygen to accept electrons and combine with hydrogen ions, NADH and FADH2 cannot dump their electrons, halting their recycling back into NAD+ and FAD.

flashcards.q: Why do NADH and FADH2 molecules yield different amounts of ATP when they donate electrons to the ETC?
flashcards.a: NADH enters the ETC at an earlier complex (higher energy state), allowing it to pump more protons and yield 3 ATP, whereas FADH2 enters later (lower energy state), yielding only 2 ATP.

8.outline_blanks: The electron transport chain, located in the mitochondrial [[cristae]], receives electrons from NADH and FADH2. These electrons are passed along carrier proteins, including iron-containing [[cytochromes]]. The final electron acceptor is [[oxygen]], which combines with hydrogen ions to form water.

8.title: ATP generation
cheat_card: ATP is generated via substrate-level phosphorylation (glycolysis & Krebs) and oxidative phosphorylation (chemiosmosis).
ETC complexes pump $H^+$ from the matrix into the intermembrane space, building an electrochemical proton gradient.
Protons diffuse down their gradient back into the matrix through the channel of ATP synthase, powering ATP synthesis.
Aerobic respiration has a 39% energy efficiency rate (harvesting 263 kcal of glucose's 686 kcal in 36 ATP), with the rest lost as heat.
8.memory_anchor:
Chemiosmosis:
Protons ($H^+$) pumped to Intermembrane Space -> Proton Motive Force -> Flow through ATP Synthase (like water through a turbine) -> Matrix -> ATP produced.

flashcards.q: How is the hydrogen ion ($H^+$) gradient established in the mitochondrion, and where is it most concentrated?
flashcards.a: The energy released from electrons flowing down the ETC is used by protein complexes to pump H+ from the matrix into the intermembrane space, where it becomes highly concentrated.

flashcards.q: Describe how ATP synthase utilizes the H+ gradient to generate ATP.
flashcards.a: ATP synthase contains a channel that allows H+ to flow down their electrochemical gradient back into the matrix. This flow of protons drives the enzyme to synthesize ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi).

flashcards.q: Calculate the approximate energy efficiency of aerobic cellular respiration if one mole of glucose contains 686 kcal and yields 36 ATP.
flashcards.a: Since each ATP phosphate bond stores 7.3 kcal, 36 ATP molecules yield 263 kcal. The efficiency is calculated as (263 / 686) * 100 = 39%, with the remaining 61% released as heat.

8.outline_blanks: During cellular respiration, the ETC pumps protons from the matrix into the [[intermembrane space]] to form a gradient. Protons then diffuse back through the [[ATP synthase]] channel to power phosphorylation. Aerobic respiration of one glucose molecule yields 36-38 ATP, representing an efficiency of [[39%]].

8.title: Bond energy
cheat_card: Catabolism includes exergonic reactions that break down molecules; anabolism includes endergonic reactions that build them.
Breaking a phosphate bond in ATP releases 7.3 kcal/mol of energy, which is used to power cellular work.
Complete oxidation of glucose yields 686 kcal, released step-wise to capture energy efficiently as ATP.
Prior to entering respiration, proteins are broken into amino acids and undergo deamination in the liver, producing toxic ammonia ($NH_3$).
Adult humans can synthesize 11 of 20 amino acids; the other 9 essential amino acids must be consumed in the diet.

Amino Acid Breakdown:
Deamination (in liver) -> Amino Group ($NH_2$) removed -> Ammonia ($NH_3$, toxic) -> Urea (excreted). Remaining carbon skeleton enters glycolysis/Krebs.

flashcards.q: Contrast catabolic (degradative) and anabolic (synthetic) reactions in terms of energy consumption and release.
flashcards.a: Catabolic reactions are exergonic (they break down molecules and release energy), whereas anabolic reactions are endergonic (they build molecules and consume energy).

flashcards.q: Explain the process of deamination of amino acids, including where it occurs and its toxic byproducts.
flashcards.a: Deamination is the removal of the amino group (NH2) from amino acids, occurring in the liver. It produces highly toxic ammonia (NH3), which the liver rapidly converts to less harmful urea for excretion.

flashcards.q: What are essential amino acids, and how many must be obtained directly from the diet of an adult human?
flashcards.a: Essential amino acids are amino acids that cannot be synthesized by the body and must be consumed. Adult humans can synthesize 11 amino acids but must obtain the remaining 9 essential amino acids from their diet.

When glucose is catabolized, it yields 686 kcal, part of which is stored in ATP phosphate bonds that release [[7.3]] kcal/mol when broken. Excess proteins undergo [[deamination]] in the liver to remove amino groups, producing toxic ammonia before their carbon chains are oxidized.

option_a.prompt: Explain the Endosymbiotic Theory regarding the origins of mitochondria and chloroplasts. Discuss the evolutionary process and describe three specific pieces of structural, genetic, or functional evidence from class notes that support this theory.
option_a.model_answer: The endosymbiotic theory proposes that mitochondria and chloroplasts evolved when a large ancestral eukaryotic cell engulfed independent prokaryotes in a symbiotic relationship. Over time, these prokaryotes became specialized organelles. Strong evidence supports this theory: first, both organelles are bound by double-layer membranes, reflecting the host vesicle and the engulfed cell's outer membrane. Second, they contain their own DNA, which exists as a single circular chromosome similar to prokaryotic genomes. Third, they contain their own ribosomes for protein building. Finally, both reproduce independently through a process resembling binary fission and can only arise from pre-existing mitochondria and chloroplasts.

option_b.prompt: Describe the step-by-step process of the endomembrane system's secretion pathway in eukaryotic cells. Detail the organelles involved and explain how they interact to synthesize, modify, label, and export proteins from the cell.
option_b.model_answer: The secretion pathway of the endomembrane system begins when ribosomes synthesize proteins on the rough ER, where the polypeptide chains fold into their functional three-dimensional shapes. These proteins are then packaged into transport vesicles that pinch off from the rough ER and travel to the Golgi apparatus. The vesicles fuse with the cis facing sacs of the Golgi, and the proteins are transported through its flattened membranous cisternae. As they pass through, the Golgi modifies the proteins (such as by adding carbohydrate labels) and sorts them. Finally, the finished proteins are packaged into new secretory vesicles that bud from the Golgi, migrate to, and merge with the plasma membrane to release their contents outside the cell via exocytosis/secretion.

option_a.prompt: Explain the steps and molecular components involved in transcription and translation in eukaryotic cells, detailing the processes and cellular locations, including post-transcriptional modifications.
option_a.model_answer: Transcription occurs in the nucleus where RNA polymerase binds to a promoter on the DNA template and synthesizes a pre-mRNA transcript in the 5' to 3' direction. Eukaryotic pre-mRNA must undergo RNA processing before exiting the nucleus, which involves adding a 5' modified Guanine cap and a 3' poly-A tail, and splicing by the spliceosome to remove non-coding introns and join coding exons. The mature mRNA then enters the cytoplasm for translation. Here, the ribosome (large and small subunits) binds the mRNA and reads it in triplet codons starting at AUG. Transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules carry specific amino acids to the ribosome, matching their complementary anticodon to the mRNA codon. The ribosome catalyzes peptide bond formation between amino acids, elongating the polypeptide chain until a stop codon triggers release of the finished protein.

option_b.prompt: Describe how the prokaryotic lac operon regulates gene expression in both the repressed (off) and induced (on) states, detailing the roles of all regulatory components.
option_b.model_answer: The lac operon is an inducible system that controls the expression of lactose-metabolizing enzymes in prokaryotes. In the repressed state, which occurs in the absence of lactose, the regulator gene produces an active repressor protein that binds tightly to the operator region. This physical block prevents RNA polymerase from binding to the promoter, turning transcription of the structural genes off. In the induced state, when lactose is present in the environment, lactose acts as an inducer by binding directly to the repressor. This binding causes a shape change that inactivates the repressor, causing it to fall off the operator. With the operator clear, RNA polymerase is free to bind to the promoter and transcribe the structural genes (lacZ, lacY, lacA) to produce the enzymes needed to metabolize lactose.

prompt_heredity_heredity_a.title: Meiosis & Genetic Variation
prompt_heredity_heredity_a.prompt: Describe the stages of meiosis I and meiosis II. Explain how independent assortment, crossing-over, and random fertilization contribute to genetic variation in offspring.
prompt_heredity_heredity_a.mnemonic: C.I.R. (Crossing over during Prophase I, Independent assortment during Anaphase I, Random union of gametes during fertilization)
prompt_heredity_heredity_a.model_answer: Meiosis is a two-step nuclear division process that reduces chromosome number from diploid to haploid, producing four genetically unique haploid gametes. In Prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair lengthwise in a process called synapsis, forming a tetrad. Non-sister chromatids twist and exchange genetic material during crossing-over, resulting in genetic recombination. During Anaphase I, independent assortment occurs as homologous chromosomes separate randomly and migrate to opposite poles, creating new combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes in the haploid cells. Following Meiosis II, which separates sister chromatids, genetic diversity is further expanded in sexual reproduction by random fertilization, the union of unique male and female gametes to form a diploid zygote.

prompt_heredity_heredity_b.title: Extensions of Mendelian Genetics
prompt_heredity_heredity_b.prompt: Explain how codominance, incomplete dominance, and pleiotropy extend the range of Mendelian genetics. Provide a specific human example for each mechanism and describe the underlying genetics.
prompt_heredity_heredity_b.mnemonic: C.I.P. (Codominance = both alleles expressed, Incomplete dominance = intermediate phenotype, Pleiotropy = one gene affects multiple traits)
prompt_heredity_heredity_b.model_answer: Inheritance patterns often extend beyond simple Mendelian dominant-recessive rules. In codominance, more than one allele is fully expressed in a heterozygote. A prime human example is ABO blood types, where the IA and IB alleles are codominant, leading to the expression of both the A and B antigen on red blood cells of IAIB individuals. In incomplete dominance, the heterozygote exhibits a phenotype that is intermediate between the two homozygotes. For example, in Familial Hypercholesterolemia, heterozygotes have an intermediate level of blood cholesterol and suffer early adulthood heart attacks, while mutant homozygotes have severe childhood heart attacks. Finally, pleiotropy occurs when a single mutated gene affects multiple, seemingly unrelated physical traits. This is demonstrated in Marfan syndrome, where a mutation in the fibrillin (FBN1) gene on chromosome 15 disrupts connective tissue, causing disproportionately long limbs, a weakened aorta, and poor eyesight.

option_a.prompt: Describe the process of speciation, distinguishing between allopatric and sympatric speciation, and explain the roles of prezygotic and postzygotic isolating mechanisms in maintaining species boundaries.
option_a.model_answer: Speciation is the splitting of one species into two or more new species. Allopatric speciation occurs when two populations of a species become geographically isolated and diverge over time due to different selection pressures. In contrast, sympatric speciation occurs without geographic isolation, often in plants through polyploidy (such as autoploidy or alloploidy), which immediately restricts breeding. Both modes rely on reproductive isolation to maintain species boundaries. This isolation is achieved via prezygotic isolating mechanisms (like habitat, temporal, behavioral, mechanical, or gamete isolation), which prevent mating attempts or fertilization. If mating occurs, postzygotic mechanisms (such as hybrid inviability or hybrid sterility) prevent hybrid offspring from developing or reproducing, ensuring the gene pools remain distinct.

option_b.prompt: Explain the concept of Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium, state the five conditions required to maintain it, and describe how deviations from these conditions lead to microevolution.
option_b.model_answer: The Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium states that allele frequencies in a population remain constant over time, indicating that no evolution is occurring. To maintain this equilibrium, five conditions must be met: no mutations, no migration (gene flow), random mating, no genetic drift, and no natural selection. In wild populations, these conditions are never fully met, and deviations lead to microevolution. For instance, random mutations introduce new alleles. Gene flow moves alleles between populations. Genetic drift causes chance changes in allele frequencies, particularly in small populations, often following a bottleneck event or a founder effect. Furthermore, nonrandom mating alters genotype frequencies, and natural selection favors individuals with higher fitness, shifting allele frequencies toward adaptive traits.

prompt_a.title: Plant Transport Systems and Transpirational Pull
prompt_a.prompt:
A botanist is studying the effects of climate change on soybean plants (Glycine max). She subjects the plants to simulated drought conditions by withholding water and raising the temperature, then monitors stomatal resistance and xylem sap tension.

1. Detail the cellular mechanism by which guard cells open and close stomata, explaining the roles of active transport of potassium ions (K+), water potential (\Psi), and the plant hormone abscisic acid (ABA).
2. Explain how the cohesion-tension theory accounts for the movement of water from the soil, through the xylem vessels, and out into the atmosphere, specifying the roles of hydrogen bonding, adhesion, and negative pressure.
3. Predict the physiological trade-off the plant faces under drought conditions, explaining how closing stomata affects both the rate of photosynthesis and the internal leaf temperature.
prompt_a.model_answer:
1. Stomatal movement is driven by turgor pressure changes in guard cells. To open stomata, H+-ATPases actively pump protons (H+) out of the guard cells, generating an electrochemical gradient. This drives the passive influx of potassium ions (K+) and chloride ions (Cl-) into the cells. The high solute concentration lowers the osmotic water potential (\Psi_s) inside the guard cells, causing water to enter via aquaporins. The guard cells swell and, because their inner cell walls are thicker and more rigid, they bow outward, opening the pore. Under drought stress, roots synthesize the hormone abscisic acid (ABA), which travels to the leaves. ABA binds to receptors on guard cells, triggering an influx of calcium ions (Ca2+) which inhibits the proton pump and opens anion channels. This depolarizes the membrane, causing K+ to exit the cell. Water follows K+ out by osmosis, the guard cells lose turgidity, and the stomata close.

2. The cohesion-tension theory explains water movement through the xylem. Transpiration occurs when water vapor diffuses out of stomata. As water evaporates from the mesophyll cell walls, it creates a high negative pressure (tension) at the air-water interface within the leaf. Because water molecules are linked by hydrogen bonds, they exhibit high cohesion. This allows the pulling force (tension) generated by evaporation to be transmitted continuously down the entire water column in the xylem, from the leaves to the roots. Adhesion, the hydrogen bonding of water molecules to the hydrophilic cellulose walls of the xylem vessels, counteracts the downward pull of gravity, keeping the water column intact and preventing cavitation.

3. The plant faces a severe physiological trade-off under drought. Closing stomata is critical to prevent lethal dehydration. However, closed stomata prevent carbon dioxide (CO2) from entering the leaf mesophyll. Without CO2, the Calvin cycle of photosynthesis stops, reducing the production of G3P and glucose. Furthermore, transpiration provides evaporative cooling to the leaf. When transpiration stops, the plant cannot dissipate solar heat, causing the internal leaf temperature to rise. This heat stress can damage photosystem proteins and denature metabolic enzymes, further impairing cellular function.
prompt_a.mnemonic: Guard stomata open when K+ goes IN and water follows. ABA lets K+ OUT to close during drought stress.

prompt_b.title: Neurophysiology, Synaptic Transmission, and Muscle Contraction
prompt_b.prompt:
A clinical researcher investigates the effects of a neurotoxin, Saxitoxin (produced by toxic dinoflagellates in 'red tides'), on motor neurons and skeletal muscle cells. Saxitoxin is a highly selective blocker of voltage-gated sodium channels in excitable membranes.

1. Describe how the resting membrane potential of a neuron is established and maintained, specifying the roles of the Na+/K+ ATPase pump and potassium leak channels.
2. Explain step-by-step how an action potential is generated and propagated down an axon, and predict the immediate effect of Saxitoxin on this process.
3. Trace how a failure in action potential propagation prevents skeletal muscle contraction, linking the synapse (neuromuscular junction), the release of acetylcholine (ACh), calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and the sliding filament theory.
prompt_b.model_answer:
1. The resting membrane potential (typically -70 mV) is established and maintained by two key membrane proteins. First, the active Na+/K+ ATPase pump utilizes ATP to transport three sodium ions (Na+) out of the cell for every two potassium ions (K+) it imports. This creates steep concentration gradients for both ions. Second, the membrane contains abundant potassium leak channels, which are always open. Because of the concentration gradient, K+ ions passively diffuse out of the cell. As positive charges leave, they leave behind unpaired negative organic anions (like proteins and phosphates) in the cytoplasm, creating a net negative charge inside the cell relative to the outside.

2. An action potential begins when a stimulus depolarizes the membrane to a threshold potential (around -55 mV). This causes voltage-gated Na+ channels to open rapidly, allowing Na+ to rush into the cell down its electrochemical gradient, depolarizing the membrane to +40 mV. At this peak, the Na+ channels inactivate, and voltage-gated K+ channels open, allowing K+ to rush out of the cell, repolarizing it. The membrane briefly hyperpolarizes before returning to rest. Saxitoxin blocks the pore of voltage-gated Na+ channels. Consequently, when a stimulus occurs, Na+ ions cannot enter the cell, preventing the depolarization phase. The membrane cannot reach threshold, and the action potential is completely blocked.

3. When action potential propagation fails, skeletal muscle contraction is prevented through the following cascade:
- At the neuromuscular junction, the absence of an action potential prevents the depolarization-induced opening of voltage-gated calcium channels in the axon terminal.
- Without calcium influx into the terminal, synaptic vesicles containing the neurotransmitter acetylcholine (ACh) cannot undergo exocytosis into the synaptic cleft.
- The muscle sarcolemma receives no ACh signal, so its ligand-gated ion channels remain closed, preventing a muscle action potential.
- Without a muscle action potential traveling down the T-tubules, voltage-sensitive receptors fail to open calcium release channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR).
- In the absence of cytoplasmic calcium, troponin remains in its default conformation, keeping tropomyosin positioned over the active binding sites on the actin thin filaments. Myosin heads cannot form cross-bridges with actin, halting the sliding filament mechanism and causing flaccid paralysis.
prompt_b.mnemonic: Saxitoxin shuts down Sodium channels, Stopping synaptic Acetylcholine release, preventing Sarcoplasmic calcium flow, and freezing the sliding filament cycle.

option_a.prompt: Explain the flow of energy and concentration of toxins through trophic pyramids, referencing the laws of thermodynamics and biomagnification.
option_a.model_answer: Energy flows unidirectionally through an ecosystem across various trophic levels, starting with primary producers (autotrophs) and moving up to primary, secondary, and tertiary consumers. According to the laws of thermodynamics, energy transfers are inefficient, with approximately 90% of energy lost as heat at each transition, meaning only about 10% is transferred to the next level. This limit on energy transfer reduces biomass at higher levels. Conversely, persistent pollutants cannot be easily metabolized or excreted; thus, they undergo biomagnification, increasing in concentration as they are consumed up the food chain, resulting in the highest toxic loads in apex predators.

option_b.prompt: Compare and contrast the electron transport chains (ETCs) of photosynthesis and cellular respiration, detailing their cellular locations, electron donors, final electron acceptors, and mechanisms of ATP generation.
option_b.model_answer: The electron transport chains of photosynthesis and cellular respiration both utilize chemiosmosis but differ in their components and location. In photosynthesis, the ETC is located in the thylakoid membrane; light energy drives the process, water serves as the initial electron donor (releasing oxygen), and NADP+ acts as the final electron acceptor to form NADPH. Protons are pumped from the stroma into the thylakoid space. In cellular respiration, the ETC is located in the mitochondrial cristae; high-energy electrons are donated by NADH and FADH2 (derived from glucose), and oxygen serves as the final electron acceptor (forming water). Protons are pumped from the matrix into the intermembrane space. In both systems, the resulting proton gradient drives ATP synthesis as protons diffuse back through the ATP synthase channel.
